  characterizing_goal: "Pupils aged 6 to 9 understand and compare simple fractions."
  claims:
    SG-01: {statement: "Every garden plot is a fraction task; decorations never interrupt a task.", evidence: [docs/design-document.md]}
    SG-03: {statement: "Paths only open when a fraction task is solved; there is no way around them.", evidence: [docs/design-document.md]}
    SG-09: {statement: "Playtested with two classes (41 pupils); most wanted to keep playing.", evidence: [docs/playtest-summary.md]}
    SG-18: {statement: "Designed by game designers with two primary teachers and a maths education researcher.", evidence: [docs/design-document.md]}

docs/design-document.md:
# Garden of Numbers: design document (example)

## Goal
Pupils aged 6 to 9 understand and compare simple fractions.

## Learning in the game
Each garden plot is split into equal parts. To plant, the pupil chooses the fraction the task asks for.
Paths to new plots open only when a task is solved. Decorations appear between tasks, never during one.

## Team
Two game designers, two primary teachers and a maths education researcher worked together from the first
prototype. Pupils tested each version.
docs/playtest-summary.md:
# Playtest summary (example)

Two classes, 41 pupils, two sessions each. Pupils understood the task without a tutorial after the first plot.
Most wanted to keep playing. Changes made: larger targets on tablets, slower plant animation.

    meaning: "Three failed attempts and a help request in the same unit within five minutes."
    fields:
      unit: {type: id}

# Keys allowed in game_state and player_metadata.

player_metadata: [age_band, captions, text_size, reduced_motion]
docs/research/agreement.md:
# Research agreement (fictional example)

Between Example Studio (controller for the study) and Example University (research partner).

- **Purpose:** learn which fraction tasks pupils aged 6 to 9 find hard, and whether the game helps them compare fractions.
- **Classes:** only classes whose school, teacher and families agreed. They get the study build (version branch `study`).
- **Data:** events listed in docs/event-catalogue.yaml. No names, no free text, no device fingerprints.
- **Extracts for the university:** relative time, no time zone, no key. Example Studio keeps the link between player codes and accounts.
- **Ethics approval:** Example University ethics committee, ref. 2026-031.
- **Open release:** group figures only, as a csef-evidence-0.1 feed, at least 10 players and 3 classes per figure.
- **Leaving the study:** a family can withdraw at any time; the pupil keeps playing the normal build.
- **Retention:** study events deleted 12 months after the end of the study.

# Example Learning Games Alliance: Code of Conduct (fictional sample)

This is a fictional code written to test the CSEF code-of-conduct comparison. It contains gaps and conflicts on purpose.

## 1. Objectives

The objective of this code is to protect children who play learning games made by our members and to build trust with schools and parents.

## 2. Age ratings

1. Members shall display an age rating label and content descriptors prominently before download or purchase.
2. Age ratings shall consider violence, sexual content and gambling-like content.

## 3. Purchases and rewards

1. Members may offer randomised reward items purchasable with virtual currency, provided that the odds are disclosed.
2. Members should show the price of virtual currency in euro where possible.
3. Purchases by children under 13 must be approved by a parent or guardian.

## 4. Engagement

1. Push notifications may be enabled by default to remind players to return.
2. Members will not use countdown timers or false urgency to pressure children.
3. Daily streak rewards are allowed to encourage regular learning.

## 5. Communication and safety

1. Members must provide a report button and the ability to block other players in every chat.
2. Chat for players under 10 shall use predefined phrases only.
3. Members shall moderate chat using trained human moderators and automated filters.

## 6. Privacy

1. Members shall carry out a data protection impact assessment before launch.
2. Children's personal data will not be used for advertising or profiling.
3. Members shall publish a privacy notice in plain language that children can understand.

## 7. Artificial intelligence

1. AI chatbots must clearly disclose to children that they are not human.
2. Members may use conversation history to personalise AI tutors.

## 8. Compliance

Members will review this code every two years.
